note_claims.claim: The patient has had pain below the right kneecap for two months.
The patient's pain has a gradual onset without a specific injury.
The patient plays football (training three times a week plus matches) and school PE.
The patient experiences pain during and after sport and when kneeling on the knee.
The patient does not experience night pain or rest pain.
The patient has no swelling, locking, or giving way of the knee.
The patient has no pain in the hip or thigh.
The patient has no fever or weight loss.
The patient's older brother had Osgood-Schlatter disease at a similar age.
The patient has no previous joint problems.
The patient has no regular medications and no known drug allergies.
The patient has no asthma or stomach problems.
There is a tender bony prominence over the right tibial tuberosity.
There is no knee effusion.
The patient has a full range of knee movement and stable ligaments.
Both hips have a full, pain-free range of movement.
The impression is Osgood-Schlatter disease of the right knee.
The plan includes activity modification guided by pain.
The plan includes icing the knee for 15 minutes after sport.
The plan includes taking paracetamol or ibuprofen 400 mg up to three times a day with food as needed.
The plan includes referring the patient to physiotherapy for stretching exercises for thigh muscles.
The plan includes a review if the condition has not settled in six to eight weeks.
The safety-netting includes returning sooner if there is night pain, knee swelling, fever, persistent limp, or hip pain.

transcript_facts.fact: Patient reports knee pain just below the kneecap.
The patient specifies the pain is in the right knee.
The duration of the pain is about two months.
The pain started after football.
The patient trains three times a week and has a match on Saturdays.
The relative mentions the patient attends PE at school.
The patient experiences pain during and after football and when kneeling on the knee.
The patient reports no night pain.
The patient reports pain only after sport, not when resting.
The patient reports no swelling, locking, or giving way of the knee.
The patient only limps after a match.
The relative mentions the patient's brother had a similar condition (Osgood-something) at age fourteen.
The relative confirms the patient has no previous joint problems.
The patient reports no regular medications.
The patient reports no asthma or stomach problems.
Clinician examines the right knee and identifies a tender bony lump just below the kneecap, which is the tibial tuberosity.
The patient confirms the location of the lump.
Clinician examines the knee, noting no fluid, full range of movement, and stable ligaments.
The patient reports no pain when the clinician moves the right hip.
Clinician examines both hips and notes full range of movement with no pain.
Clinician provides an impression of Osgood-Schlatter disease, explaining it is an irritation where the tendon from the kneecap attaches to the shin bone.
Clinician advises the patient to cut down on activity for a few weeks and let the pain guide them.
Clinician recommends icing the knee for 15 minutes after sport.
Clinician recommends paracetamol or ibuprofen 400 milligrams up to three times a day with food for pain.
Clinician plans to refer the patient to physiotherapy for stretching exercises for thigh muscles.
Clinician outlines follow-up criteria: return sooner if there is night pain, knee swelling, fever, persistent limp, or hip pain.
